source.title: Extrapolating Large Language Models to Non-English by Aligning Languages
source.authors: Wenhao Zhu; Yunzhe Lv; Qingxiu Dong; Fei Yuan; Jingjing Xu; Shujian Huang; Lingpeng Kong; Jiajun Chen; Lei Li

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some figure contents are not available in the extracted text.
record.tranche_reason: It studies a scaling relationship in a new setting—cross-lingual instruction-tuning—and reports results for translation performance as translation-data scale changes. It does not reproduce the original held-out pretraining-loss scaling measurements.
record.gate_note: Figure 3 reports translation performance against translation-data scale and describes a fitted scaling law. Figure 7 compares scaling trends for parallel data and monolingual continued pre-training. Results on multilingual data allocation, QA, translation benchmarks, and representation alignment do not test the claim's parameter/token compute-optimal split or held-out pretraining loss, so they are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study fits a power-law-style curve, S(X)=100−α(γX)^β, to COMET translation score against translation-instruction data scale. The setting is cross-lingual instruction-tuning of LLaMA-7B, a fine-tuning regime. This bears on V5. It does not measure pretraining loss against parameters, tokens or compute.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors' main conclusions concern CoIT/MuIT gains: +27.83% on QA over Alpaca-7B, +18.89% on translation, m-LLaMA matching x-LLaMAs, and middle-layer alignment. The scaling law is a secondary tool, shown to fit the trend and to support data allocation. The allocation gains were minor at a low budget and significant only at 1.2M.
record.recipe_differences: The study fits a bounded power-law-style formulation to translation performance versus translation-data scale during cross-lingual instruction-tuning. It does not measure held-out pretraining loss versus model parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The formulation includes a language-similarity factor, and the paper compares parallel-data instruction-tuning with monolingual continued pre-training; the extracted text gives no per-language fitted values.

fits_no_version.finding: Allocating translation data with the fitted laws beats uniform allocation only slightly. The gain is +0.25 COMET at a 300k budget (minor) and +0.48 COMET at 1.2M (significant at p<0.1) (Table 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling laws fitted per language in instruction-tuning can guide multi-language data allocation under a fixed data budget, with small gains.

fits_no_version.finding: Parallel-data instruction-tuning is reported as far more data-efficient than monolingual continued pre-training for translation/semantic alignment (Figure 7).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data efficiency of scaling differs strongly by data type (parallel versus monolingual) for cross-lingual alignment.

record.problems: The scaling-curve values and fitted parameters are unavailable in the extracted figure text. The reported scaling result concerns translation quality in cross-lingual instruction-tuning rather than held-out pretraining loss. The text gives no uncertainty estimates for the Figure 3 scaling results.
record.rows_left_out: Section 5.2, Table 4 reports optimized versus uniform allocation of translation data across languages, not a parameter/token allocation at fixed compute. Other benchmark and ablation results do not measure a version of the claim.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolation from small fitted runs to much larger runs.
Parameter/token compute-optimal split. The allocation studied is translation data across languages.
Architecture shape at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities, loss as the measure, and model-size scaling. Only data scale in instruction-tuning at 7B is tested.
Downstream performance versus model scale or pretraining loss.
Sensitivity of exponents to fitting choices, and bending away from a power law.

record.verdict_notes: The record marks uncertainty_reported 'y', but no uncertainty is given for the scaling fits; only Table 4 has a p<0.1 marker. The functional form is built with a fixed ceiling of 100 and a language-similarity factor. 'Power law' here describes the gap to the maximum score of a downstream metric, not loss. The V5 support is therefore loose and rests on author wording over figure-only data.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss against parameter count, training tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted on smaller runs.

The compute-optimal split between model parameters and training tokens, and how each grows with compute. The paper optimizes translation-data allocation across languages, not parameters versus tokens.
Effects of architecture details such as depth and width at fixed parameter count.
Tests translation performance as translation-data scale changes during cross-lingual instruction-tuning, not held-out pretraining loss; no other modalities are tested.
Predictability of downstream-task performance from model scale or pretraining loss.
Whether exponents or compute-optimal splits vary with fitting choices, and whether curves systematically bend away from a single power law.

rows.measure: Translation performance (COMET) as a function of translation-data scale; the authors report that added translation data is beneficial and that their scaling-law formulation captures the trend.
rows.note: The authors give the qualitative result in the text, but the plotted values and estimated laws are not present in the extracted figure content. This is translation performance, not held-out pretraining loss.
rows.check: The state rests only on the authors' wording ('fits well with the trend'). Fitted α and β, data points and the per-language breakdown are in Figure 3 and not in the text. The measure is a bounded downstream metric (COMET gap to 100), not held-out loss.

relationships.condition: LLaMA-7B cross-lingual instruction-tuning, COMET versus translation-data scale, six languages
relationships.reason: Authors report that adding translation data always helps and that their bounded power-law formulation fits the trend (r1). The evidence is qualitative only: fit values are figure-only and no uncertainty is given.
relationships.display_finding: Adding translation data consistently improved COMET across six languages, with the authors reporting a bounded power-law fit.
